questions.questionText: Let \( W_1, W_2, W_3 \) be three distinct subspaces of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \) such that each \( W_i \) has dimension \( 9 \). Let \[ W = W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3 . \] Then we can conclude that— \( W \) may not be a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \). \( \dim (W) \le 8 \). \( \dim (W) \ge 7 \). \( \dim (W) \le 3 \).
questions.questionHtml:
Let \( W_1, W_2, W_3 \) be three distinct subspaces of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \) such that each \( W_i \) has dimension \( 9 \). Let \[ W = W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3 . \] Then we can conclude that—

  1. \( W \) may not be a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \).
     
  2. \( \dim (W) \le 8 \).
     
  3. \( \dim (W) \ge 7 \).
     
  4. \( \dim (W) \le 3 \).

options.label: A
options.text: \( W \) may not be a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \).

questions.explanation: Since \( W_1, W_2 \), and \( W_3 \) are subspaces of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \), their intersection \( W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3 \) is also a subspace of \( \mathbb{R}^{10} \) (arbitrary intersection of subspaces is a subspace). Hence, option (1) is false. Given that \[ \dim (W_1) = \dim (W_2) = \dim (W_3) = 9 . \] For a subspace \( W_i \subset \mathbb{R}^{10} \), \[ \dim (W_i) = \dim (\mathbb{R}^{10}) - \text{number of linearly independent restrictions}. \] Therefore, \[ 9 = 10 - \text{number of linearly independent restrictions}, \] which implies that each \( W_i \) has exactly one linearly independent restriction. Since the subspaces \( W_1, W_2 \), and \( W_3 \) are distinct, the total number of linearly independent restrictions defining \( W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3 \) is \( 3 \). Hence, \[ \dim (W_1 \cap W_2 \cap W_3) = 10 - 3 = 7 . \] Thus, options (2) and (3) are true, and option (4) is false. questions.explanation: Since \( A = U \Sigma V^T \) with \( \text{rank}(A) = n \), the matrix \( V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \) is a square matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of \( \mathbb{R}^n \). Hence, \[ V^T = V^{-1}, \] which implies \[ (V^T)^{-1} = V. \] Therefore, option (A) is false . Now, \[ A^T A = (U \Sigma V^T)^T (U \Sigma V^T) = V \Sigma U^T U \Sigma V^T. \] Since \( U^T U = I_n \) and \( \Sigma^T = \Sigma \), we obtain \[ A^T A = V \Sigma^2 V^T, \] so option (B) is correct . questions.explanation: Since \( A \) is non-singular, for any non-zero vector \( x \in \mathbb{R}^n \), \( x^{T} A A^{T} x = (A^{T}x)^{T}(A^{T}x) = \|A^{T}x\|^{2} > 0. \) Thus, the matrix \( A A^{T} \) is symmetric and positive definite. Since \( B = A^{T} \), we have \( AB = A A^{T}. \) Hence, among the given options, only \( AB \) is necessarily positive definite. questions.questionText: Minimum of dimension of the intersection of two seven dimensional vector subspaces in a twelve dimensional vector space is:
questions.questionHtml: Minimum of dimension of the intersection of two seven dimensional vector subspaces in a twelve dimensional vector space is:
questions.explanation: Let \( V \) be a vector space of dimension \( 12 \). Let \( S \) and \( T \) be two subspaces of \( V \), each of dimension \( 7 \). First look at the subspace \( S \). It already uses \( 7 \) independent directions of \( V \). So, outside \( S \), only \[ 12 - 7 = 5 \] independent directions are left. Now build the subspace \( T \). At most \( 5 \) independent vectors of \( T \) can be chosen outside \( S \). Since \( T \) has dimension \( 7 \), the remaining \[ 7 - 5 = 2 \] vectors must lie inside \( S \). This means \( S \) and \( T \) must have at least two common independent vectors. Hence, the minimum possible value of \( \dim(S \cap T) \) is \[ \boxed{2} \] GO Classes answered Jan 3 • edited Jan 3 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. All arithmetic is performed modulo 2 , that is, \( 1 + 1 = 0. \) Suppose that \( \operatorname{tr}(A) = \operatorname{tr}(B) \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(B^2). \) Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true? \(A\) and \(B\) have the same eigenvalues \(A\) and \(B\) have the same determinant \(A\) and \(B\) may have different eigenvalues \(A = B\)
questions.questionHtml:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be \(2 \times 2\) matrices whose entries belong to \(\{0,1\}\).

All arithmetic is performed modulo 2, that is, \( 1 + 1 = 0. \)

Suppose that \( \operatorname{tr}(A) = \operatorname{tr}(B) \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(B^2). \)

Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true?

  1. \(A\) and \(B\) have the same eigenvalues
  2. \(A\) and \(B\) have the same determinant
  3. \(A\) and \(B\) may have different eigenvalues
  4. \(A = B\)
questions.explanation: The given conditions state that the matrices \(A\) and \(B\) have the same trace and the same trace of their squares, with all arithmetic performed modulo 2 (that is, \(1+1=0\)). Consider the matrices \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] We compute the traces: \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 0\) \(\operatorname{tr}(B) = 1 + 1 = 0\) Next, we compute the traces of the squares: \(A^2 = A \Rightarrow \operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(A) = 0\) \(B^2 = B \Rightarrow \operatorname{tr}(B^2) = \operatorname{tr}(B) = 0\) Thus, both conditions \( \operatorname{tr}(A) = \operatorname{tr}(B) \quad \text{and} \quad \operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(B^2) \) are satisfied. However, the eigenvalues are: Eigenvalues of \(A\): \(\{0,0\}\) Eigenvalues of \(B\): \(\{1,1\}\) Hence, the eigenvalues are different. Option C . questions.explanation: Let \[ A=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad Q(x)=x^T A x,\; x\in\mathbb{R}^3. \] The matrix \(A\) is symmetric, so all its eigenvalues are real. The sign of the quadratic form \(Q(x)\) depends on the signs of these eigenvalues. The trace of \(A\) is \[ \operatorname{tr}(A)=3+2+1=6, \] which equals the sum of the eigenvalues. The determinant of \(A\) is \[ \det(A)= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} =-18. \] Hence, \[ \lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3=-18<0, \] so at least one eigenvalue is negative. Moreover, \[ \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1\\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} =5>0, \] and the trace is positive, while the determinant is negative. Therefore, the matrix has exactly two positive eigenvalues and one negative eigenvalue. Since \(A\) has a negative eigenvalue, there exists some \(x\in\mathbb{R}^3\) such that \(Q(x)<0\). \[ \boxed{\text{Statements (a) and (d) are true.}} \]

questions.questionText: Let $S$ and $T$ be vector subspaces of a vector space $V$. Then $S \cup T$ is a subspace of $V$ is never true if and only if one of $S$ or $T$ is trivial if and only if $S \subseteq T$ or $T \subseteq S$ if and only if $S \cap T$ is a nonzero vector space.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $S$ and $T$ be vector subspaces of a vector space $V$. Then $S \cup T$ is a subspace of $V$

  1. is never true
     
  2. if and only if one of $S$ or $T$ is trivial
     
  3. if and only if $S \subseteq T$ or $T \subseteq S$
     
  4. if and only if $S \cap T$ is a nonzero vector space.

options.label: B
options.text: if and only if one of $S$ or $T$ is trivial

options.label: C
options.text: if and only if $S \subseteq T$ or $T \subseteq S$

options.label: D
options.text: if and only if $S \cap T$ is a nonzero vector space.

questions.explanation: Let $S$ and $T$ be subspaces of a vector space $V$. For $S \cup T$ to be a subspace, it must be closed under addition. That is, for any $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, the sum $s+t$ must also belong to $S \cup T$. This is possible only if one of the subspaces is contained in the other. Hence, \[ S \cup T \text{ is a subspace if and only if } S \subseteq T \text{ or } T \subseteq S. \] This corresponds to Option~C. Why Option B is incomplete. If one of the subspaces is trivial, i.e.\ $\{0\}$, then it is contained in every subspace. In this case, \[ \{0\} \cup T = T, \] which is a subspace. Therefore, Option~B describes a valid special case. However, two subspaces can both be non-trivial and still satisfy $S \subseteq T$ or $T \subseteq S$. In such cases, their union is also a subspace, but Option~B does not include these situations.   Option~B implies Option~C but is not complete. Option~C gives the correct and full condition.

questions.questionText: Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix} \] and let \(I\) denote the \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix. If \( 6A^{-1} = aA^2 + bA + cI, \) for real numbers \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\), then the ordered triple \((a,b,c)\) is equal to: \((1,\,2,\,1)\) \((4,\,1,\,1)\) \((1,\,-1,\,2)\) \((1,\,4,\,1)\)
questions.questionHtml:
Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix} \] and let \(I\) denote the \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix.

If \( 6A^{-1} = aA^2 + bA + cI, \) for real numbers \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\), then the ordered triple \((a,b,c)\) is equal to:

  1. \((1,\,2,\,1)\)
     
  2. \((4,\,1,\,1)\)
     
  3. \((1,\,-1,\,2)\)
     
  4. \((1,\,4,\,1)\)
questions.explanation: We solve the problem using the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem . Given \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. \] Since \(A\) is a triangular matrix, its eigenvalues are \(1,\,-2,\,-3\). Hence, the characteristic polynomial of \(A\) is \((\lambda - 1)(\lambda + 2)(\lambda + 3)\), which simplifies to \[ \lambda^3 + 4\lambda^2 + \lambda - 6. \] By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, \(A^3 + 4A^2 + A - 6I = 0\). Since \(A\) is invertible, multiply both sides by \(A^{-1}\) to obtain \(A^2 + 4A + I - 6A^{-1} = 0\). Rearranging, \[ 6A^{-1} = A^2 + 4A + I. \] Comparing with \(6A^{-1} = aA^2 + bA + cI\), we get \(a = 1,\; b = 4,\; c = 1\). Therefore, the ordered triple is \((a,b,c) = (1,4,1)\). Which of the following matrices represents the orthogonal projection onto the row space of $A$ ? $\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$ $I-\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$ $\frac{v^{T} v}{v v^{T}}$ $I+\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a matrix $A$ such that its null space $N(A)$ is spanned by a nonzero vector $v$.
Which of the following matrices represents the orthogonal projection onto the row space of $A$ ?

  1. $\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$
     
  2. $I-\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$
     
  3. $\frac{v^{T} v}{v v^{T}}$
     
  4. $I+\frac{v v^{T}}{v^{T} v}$
questions.explanation: 1. Identify the Relationship Between Spaces In linear algebra, the null space $N(A)$ and the row space $C(A^T)$ of a matrix are orthogonal complements of each other. This means: Every vector in the row space is perpendicular to every vector in the null space. The entire space (let's call it $\mathbb{R}^n$) can be split into these two parts. 2. Find the Projection onto the Null Space The problem states that the null space $N(A)$ is spanned by a single nonzero vector $v$. The formula for the orthogonal projection matrix $P_{null}$ onto a line spanned by a vector $v$ is: $$P_{null} = \frac{vv^T}{v^Tv}$$ 3. Find the Projection onto the Row Space Since the row space is the orthogonal complement of the null space, any vector $x$ can be written as: $$x = P_{row}x + P_{null}x$$ To get the projection onto the row space, we subtract the projection onto the null space from the Identity matrix $I$: $$P_{row} = I - P_{null}$$ $$P_{row} = I - \frac{vv^T}{v^Tv}$$ Conclusion The correct answer is B .

  1. If the dimension of $U \cap V$ is $2$ and the dimension of $U$ is $3$, then $\left\{v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}\right\}$ is linearly dependent.
     
  2. If $U+V=\{u+v: u \in U, v \in V\}=\mathbb{R}^{4}$, then either $\left\{u_{1}, u_{2}, u_{3}\right\}$ is linearly independent or $\left\{v_{1}, v_{2}, v_{3}\right\}$ is linearly independent.
     

Which of the above statements is/are true?

  1. Only I
     
  2. Only II
     
  3. Both I and II
     
  4. Neither I nor II

questions.questionText: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ real matrix and consider the system $A x=b$. Which of the following statements are correct ? Any solution $x$ of $A x=b$ (if it exists) can be expressed as the sum of a vector from the null space of $A$ and a vector from the row space of $A$. The system $A x=b$ is solvable if and only if $b$ is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of $A$. If $A$ is a $4 \times 3$ matrix and the solutions of $A x=b$ are not unique whenever they exist, then the rank of $A$ must be exactly $2$. If $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are two solutions of $A x=b$, then $x_{1}-x_{2}$ lies in the null space of $A$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ real matrix and consider the system $A x=b$.

Which of the following statements are correct?

  1. Any solution $x$ of $A x=b$ (if it exists) can be expressed as the sum of a vector from the null space of $A$ and a vector from the row space of $A$.
     
  2. The system $A x=b$ is solvable if and only if $b$ is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of $A$.
     
  3. If $A$ is a $4 \times 3$ matrix and the solutions of $A x=b$ are not unique whenever they exist, then the rank of $A$ must be exactly $2$.
     
  4. If $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are two solutions of $A x=b$, then $x_{1}-x_{2}$ lies in the null space of $A$.

options.label: A
options.text: Any solution $x$ of $A x=b$ (if it exists) can be expressed as the sum of a vector from the null space of $A$ and a vector from the row space of $A$.

options.label: B
options.text: The system $A x=b$ is solvable if and only if $b$ is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of $A$.

options.label: C
options.text: If $A$ is a $4 \times 3$ matrix and the solutions of $A x=b$ are not unique whenever they exist, then the rank of $A$ must be exactly $2$.

options.label: D
options.text: If $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are two solutions of $A x=b$, then $x_{1}-x_{2}$ lies in the null space of $A$.

questions.explanation: Statement A: Any solution x of Ax = b can be expressed as the sum of a vector from the null space of A and a vector from the row space of A. True Reason:  For any matrix A(m*n), Row(A) and Null(A) can together span the entire R^n bcz they are orthogonal complement of each other. Since these 2 subspaces span the entire space R^n, any vector x that exists within R^n (including a solution to Ax=b) can be written as a unique sum:                                                          x = x_row + x_null,          where,  x_row is the projection of the solution onto the row space, whereas  x_null  is the projection of the solution onto the null space. Statement B: The system Ax = b is solvable if and only if b is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of A.   False Reason: The system Ax

LET'S CONVERT THIS TO THE CHARACTERISTIC POLYNOMIAL EQUATION BY CAYLEY HAMILTON THEOREM... LET EIGEN VALUE BE x....!! So, x^2 + 2.x  + 1 = 0... So, answer leads to the eigen values -1,-1... questions.questionHtml:
For $n \geq 2$, let $M(n)$ denote the ring of all $n \times n$ matrices with real entries. Which of the following statements are true?

    a. If $A \in M(2)$ is nilpotent and non-zero, then there exists a matrix $B \in          M(2)$   such that $B^2 = A$.

    b. If $A \in M(n)$, $n \geq 2$, is symmetric and positive definite, then there exists a symmetric matrix $B \in M(n)$ such that $B^2 = A$.

    c. If $A \in M(n)$, $n \geq 2$, is symmetric, then there exists a symmetric matrix $B \in M(n)$ such that $B^3 = A$.
questions.explanation: Option A: False Claim: $A \in M(2)$ is nilpotent and non-zero.  Then: For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the ``power of nilpotency'' is 2.  If $A$ is nilpotent, $A^2 = 0$.  Non-Zero Claim is False. Option B: False Symmetric Positive Definite (PD) matrix = Positive Eigenvalues ($\lambda > 0$). Now, we can always take the square root of a positive eigenvalue. Actually, PD means eigenvalues are "safe" for square roots.  Hence, $B$ will always exist and be symmetric. Option C: True Real Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues. You can take the cube root ($\sqrt[3]{\lambda}$) of any real number (positive, negative, or zero) and get a real result. Since eigenvalues are real, $B$ always exists.  Only requires real eigenvalues (Symmetric). soudipta_dutta answered Nov 24, 2025 • edited Apr 8 by soudipta_dutta soudipta_dutta comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. a. The determinant of $A$ is a rational number.

questions.explanation: Orthogonal Matrix : It's a Solid Brick.   Option A :  True det(A) = Ration Number. = True The determinant of a rigid body(A Brick) is just the volume-scale factor. A_1:   +1 (Spun / Rotation): The brick is rotated, moved, or turned. The orientation stays the same (right-handed remains right-handed). The volume changes by a factor of 1, meaning the volume is preserved. A_2   : −1 (Mirrored / Reflection): The brick is mirrored (e.g., in a mirror, it would look like a left-handed version of itself). The orientation is reversed (handedness flips). However, the volume still changes by a factor of 1 (strictly speaking, the absolute value is 1), meaning the amount of space it occupies remains identical despite the reversal.   This is Why Option C is False. The solid brick is "rigid." It can turn around (+1) or it can be reflected (-1), but it cannot be squashed, stretched, or have its total volume increased or decrease. Since, 1 and −1 are rational numbers. It's True

Notation:

\( \mathbb{R}^n \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C}^n \)) denotes the \( n \)-dimensional Euclidean space over \( \mathbb{R} \) (respectively, over \( \mathbb{C} \)), and is assumed to be endowed with its `usual' topology.

Which of the following sets are compact in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \) ?
a. The set of all upper triangular matrices all of whose eigenvalues satisfy
    $|λ| ≤ 2$
b. The set of all real symmetric matrices all of whose eigenvalues satisfy
     $|λ| ≤ 2$

questions.explanation: Option A :  Here $A$ is an Upper Triangular Matrix.  $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \text{HUGE_NUMBER} \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$  Eigenvalues (1 and 2) less than or equal to 2 HUGE_NUMBER can go to infinity NOT BOUNDED and NOT COMPACT  Option b : For a symmetric matrix, the size of its largest eigenvalue (max$|\lambda|$) = overall ``size'' (norm) of the matrix.  max$|\lambda|$ = $\|A\|_2$ (the spectral norm)  $|\lambda| \leq 2$ directly forces the matrix's norm to be small ($\|A\|_2 \leq 2$)  CLOSED and BOUNDED. Therefore, it is COMPACT. Option c.   Diagonalizable is a Non-Closed property. If $A_k = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 + \varepsilon \end{bmatrix}$ For any $\varepsilon \neq 0$, the eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\lambda_2 = 1 + \varepsilon$ are distinct. Hence, diagonalizable If $\varepsilon \to 0$,  then it becomes non-diagonalizable matrix: $J = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ Hence, NOT COMP

questions.questionText: Notation: \( \mathbb{R}^n \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C}^n \)) denotes the \( n \)-dimensional Euclidean space over \( \mathbb{R} \) (respectively, over \( \mathbb{C} \)), and is assumed to be endowed with its `usual' topology.   \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \) (respectively, \( M_n(\mathbb{C}) \)) will denote the set of all \( n \times n \) matrices with entries from \( \mathbb{R} \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C} \)) and is identified with \( \mathbb{R}^{n^2} \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C}^{n^2} \)) when considered as a topological space. Let \[ S = \{ A \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) : \operatorname{tr}(A) = 0 \}. \] Which of the following statements are true?     a. \( S \) is nowhere dense in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).     b. \( S \) is connected in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).     c. \( S \) is compact in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).
questions.questionHtml:
Notation:

\( \mathbb{R}^n \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C}^n \)) denotes the \( n \)-dimensional Euclidean space over \( \mathbb{R} \) (respectively, over \( \mathbb{C} \)), and is assumed to be endowed with its `usual' topology.  
\( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \) (respectively, \( M_n(\mathbb{C}) \)) will denote the set of all \( n \times n \) matrices with entries from \( \mathbb{R} \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C} \)) and is identified with \( \mathbb{R}^{n^2} \) (respectively, \( \mathbb{C}^{n^2} \)) when considered as a topological space.

Let
\[
S = \{ A \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) : \operatorname{tr}(A) = 0 \}.
\]
Which of the following statements are true?

    a. \( S \) is nowhere dense in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).
    b. \( S \) is connected in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).
    c. \( S \) is compact in \( M_n(\mathbb{R}) \).
questions.explanation: Our universe is $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, the space of all $n \times n$ matrices, which is identified with $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$—a big, flat, Euclidean space of dimension $n^2$. The condition \[ \operatorname{tr}(A) = a_{11} + a_{22} + \cdots + a_{nn} = 0 \] defines a linear equation in the entries of $A$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$, an equation like $x + y + z = 0$ defines a flat plane passing through the origin. Similarly, in our $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ space, the equation $a_{11} + \cdots + a_{nn} = 0$ defines a flat hyperplane passing through the origin. Therefore, $S$ is a giant, flat hyperplane living inside the larger space $M_n(\mathbb{R})$. Now just remember:  Every hyperplane in a vector space of dimension $> 1$ is a classic example of a nowhere dense set.  Every hyperplane is a prime example of a connected set.  Every hyperplane in a vector space (of positive dimension) is non-compact because it is unbounded. Hence, statements (a) and (b) are TRUE, and statement (c) is FALSE

Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 19 & 2019 \\ 2019 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Which of the following statements are true? a.  The matrix \( A \) is diagonalizable over \( \mathbb{R} \).  b. There exists a basis of \( \mathbb{R}^2 \) consisting of eigenvectors \( \{ \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2 \} \) of the matrix \( A \) such that \( \mathbf{w}_1^\top \mathbf{w}_2 = 0 \).  c.  There exists a matrix \( B \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R}) \) such that \( B^3 = A \).

questions.explanation: Finding the Basis for the Orthogonal Complement $V^{\perp}$ Understanding the Problem: The matrix $A$ is: $$ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$  By definition, the null space of $A$ is the set of all vectors $\mathbf{v} = (x, y, z, t)$ such that $A \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. \[ V = \text{Null}(A) \] We seek a basis for $V^{\perp}$, which is a basis for $(\text{Null}(A))^{\perp}$. Theorem of Linear Algebra (Short Cut): $$ (\text{Null}(A))^{\perp} = \text{Row}(A) $$ Therefore,  \[ V^{\perp} = \text{Row}(A) \] The Solution:  First Row Vector (from first equation):     $$1x + 1y - 1z + 0t = 0 \quad \implies \quad \mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{(1, 1, -1, 0)}$$      Second Row Vector (from second equation):     $$1x + 1y + 0z + 1t = 0 \quad \implies \quad \mathbf{r}_2 = \mathbf{(1, 1, 0, 1)}$$ Linear Independence Check: (1, 1, -1, 0)  vs (1, 1, 0, 1)  Their zeros are in differ

questions.explanation: Rank-Nullity Theorem: For $3 \times 3$ matrices \[ \dim(\operatorname{Im}(A)) + \dim(\operatorname{Ker}(A)) = 3 \] \[ \operatorname{rank}(A) + \operatorname{nullity}(A) = 3 \] \[ \dim(\operatorname{Im}(A)) \leq \dim(\operatorname{Ker}(A)) \] \[ \operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \operatorname{nullity}(A) \] Substituting $\operatorname{nullity}(A) = 3 - \operatorname{rank}(A)$: \[ \operatorname{rank}(A) \leq 3 - \operatorname{rank}(A) \] \[ 2 \cdot \operatorname{rank}(A) \leq 3 \] $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ must be less than or equal to $1.5$. Since rank is an integer, the maximum possible rank is $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 1$. questions.explanation: To share all eigenvectors, matrices $A$ and $B = A^T A$ must commute: \[ MN = NM. \] Thus, for $A$ and $B = A^T A$ to share all eigenvectors, we require: \[ A(A^T A) = (A^T A)A. \] Compute both sides: \begin{align*} A(A^T A) &= AA^T A, \\ (A^T A)A &= A^T A^2. \end{align*} Equating them: \[ AA^T A = A^T A^2. \] Rearranging: \[ AA^T A - A^T A^2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad (AA^T - A^T A)A = 0. \] This implies that the matrix $(AA^T - A^T A)$, when applied to any vector in the image of $A$, yields zero. However, for this to hold for all vectors (i.e., for $A$ and $B$ to commute), we must have: \[ AA^T - A^T A = 0, \] or equivalently, \[ \boxed{AA^T = A^T A}. \] This condition defines a normal matrix. However, the problem states that $A$ is a general real matrix — not necessarily normal. Therefore, in general, $A$ and $A^T A$ do not commute. Hence Both statements are Wrong. Option D = Correct

questions.questionText: A new type of sensor, $ X $, is designed to measure signal strength, but its manufacturing process is flawed, causing its reading to follow a Uniform Distribution over an interval that depends entirely on a single unknown parameter $ \theta $. The probability density function (PDF) is given by: \[ f(x \mid \theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\theta^2} & \text{for } 0 \leq x \leq \theta^2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] A data scientist collects $ N $ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from this sensor: $ \mathbf{X} = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N\} $. Question: What is the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE), $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} $, for the parameter $ \theta $? Options:     (A) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i $ (The Sample Mean)     (B) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i } $ (The Method of Moments Estimator)     (C) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \sqrt{ \max(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N) } $  (Square Root of the Maximum Observation)     (D) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \sqrt{ \frac{N+1}{N} \max(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N) } $ (Unbiased Estimator)

A new type of sensor, $ X $, is designed to measure signal strength, but its manufacturing process is flawed, causing its reading to follow a Uniform Distribution over an interval that depends entirely on a single unknown parameter $ \theta $.

The probability density function (PDF) is given by:
\[
f(x \mid \theta) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{\theta^2} & \text{for } 0 \leq x \leq \theta^2 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

A data scientist collects $ N $ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from this sensor: $ \mathbf{X} = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N\} $.

 

Question: What is the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE), $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} $, for the parameter $ \theta $?

Options:

    (A) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i $ (The Sample Mean)
    (B) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i } $ (The Method of Moments Estimator)
    (C) $ \hat{\theta}_{ML} = \sqrt{ \max(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N) } $  (Square Root of the Maximum Observation)

questions.questionText: Matrix Eigenvalue Problem (HARD) Q1. Let $ A $ be an $ n \times n $ real symmetric positive definite matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n > 0 $. Let $ \mathbf{v}_1 $ and $ \mathbf{v}_n $ be the unit eigenvectors corresponding to $ \lambda_1 $ and $ \lambda_n $, respectively. Define a new matrix $ B = A + \gamma \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^T $, where $ \gamma > 0 $ and $ \mathbf{u} $ is an arbitrary non-zero real vector. Let $ \mu_1 \geq \mu_2 \geq \cdots \geq \mu_n $ be the eigenvalues of $ B $. Which of the following statements is FALSE for any choice of $ \gamma > 0 $ and non-zero vector $ \mathbf{u} $?     (A) The eigenvector corresponding to $ \mu_1 $ is orthogonal to $ \mathbf{v}_n $.     (B) $ \mu_n > \lambda_n $ and $ \mu_1 = \lambda_1 $.     (C) $ \mu_1 > \lambda_1 $ and the eigenvector corresponding to $ \mu_1 $ is parallel to $ \mathbf{v}_1 $.     (D) There exists an index $ k $ such that $ \mu_k < \lambda_k $ and $ \mu_{k+1} > \lambda_{k+1} $.
questions.questionHtml:
Matrix Eigenvalue Problem (HARD) Q1.

Let $ A $ be an $ n \times n $ real symmetric positive definite matrix with eigenvalues $ \lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n > 0 $. Let $ \mathbf{v}_1 $ and $ \mathbf{v}_n $ be the unit eigenvectors corresponding to $ \lambda_1 $ and $ \lambda_n $, respectively.

Define a new matrix $ B = A + \gamma \mathbf{u} \mathbf{u}^T $, where $ \gamma > 0 $ and $ \mathbf{u} $ is an arbitrary non-zero real vector.

Let $ \mu_1 \geq \mu_2 \geq \cdots \geq \mu_n $ be the eigenvalues of $ B $.

Which of the following statements is FALSE for any choice of $ \gamma > 0 $ and non-zero vector $ \mathbf{u} $?

    (A) The eigenvector corresponding to $ \mu_1 $ is orthogonal to $ \mathbf{v}_n $.
    (B) $ \mu_n > \lambda_n $ and $ \mu_1 = \lambda_1 $.
    (C) $ \mu_1 > \lambda_1 $ and the eigenvector corresponding to $ \mu_1 $ is parallel to $ \mathbf{v}_1 $.
    (D) There exists an index $ k $ such that $ \mu_k < \lambda_k $ and $ \mu_{k+1} > \lambda_{k+1} $.

questions.questionText: Q.29 Consider the simple linear regression model \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad i = 1, 2, \dots, n \quad (n \geq 3), \] where $ \beta_0 $ and $ \beta_1 $ are unknown parameters, $ \varepsilon_i $'s are uncorrelated random errors with mean 0 and finite variance $ \sigma^2 > 0 $. Let $ \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i $ and $ \hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i $, $ i = 1, 2, \dots, n $, where $ \hat{\beta}_0 $ and $ \hat{\beta}_1 $ represent least squares estimators of $ \beta_0 $ and $ \beta_1 $, respectively. Let \[ T_1 = \frac{1}{n-2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \quad \text{and} \quad T_2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2. \] Then which one of the following statements is true?     (A) Both $ T_1 $ and $ T_2 $ are unbiased estimators of $ \sigma^2 $.     (B) $ T_1 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $, but $ T_2 $ is not an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.     (C) $ T_1 $ is not an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $, but $ T_2 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.     (D) Neither $ T_1 $ nor $ T_2 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.
questions.questionHtml:
Q.29 Consider the simple linear regression model
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad i = 1, 2, \dots, n \quad (n \geq 3),
\]
where $ \beta_0 $ and $ \beta_1 $ are unknown parameters, $ \varepsilon_i $'s are uncorrelated random errors with mean 0 and finite variance $ \sigma^2 > 0 $. Let $ \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i $ and $ \hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i $, $ i = 1, 2, \dots, n $, where $ \hat{\beta}_0 $ and $ \hat{\beta}_1 $ represent least squares estimators of $ \beta_0 $ and $ \beta_1 $, respectively. Let
\[
T_1 = \frac{1}{n-2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \quad \text{and} \quad T_2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2.
\]
Then which one of the following statements is true?

    (A) Both $ T_1 $ and $ T_2 $ are unbiased estimators of $ \sigma^2 $.
    (B) $ T_1 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $, but $ T_2 $ is not an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.
    (C) $ T_1 $ is not an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $, but $ T_2 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.
    (D) Neither $ T_1 $ nor $ T_2 $ is an unbiased estimator of $ \sigma^2 $.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.explanation: Since we know that $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y-\hat{y})^2}{\sigma^2}$ follows $\chi_{n-2}^{2}$ $$\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y-\hat{y})^2}{\sigma^2}\right]=n-2 \implies \mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y-\hat{y})^2}{n-2}\right]=\sigma^2$$ $$\mathbb{E}[T_1] =\sigma^2$$ Hence $T_1$ solely is the unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$. option (B) is correct.

questions.explanation: Think of the simple linear regression line ($$\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i$$) as being anchored to a specific point: the mean point ($\bar{x}, \bar{y}$). The slope, $\hat{\beta}_1$, dictates how the line rotates around this point. The mean point, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, dictates the line's position on the plane. OR: Imagine a ramp built on the ground. The slope ($\hat{\beta}_1$) is the steepness of the ramp. \\ The mean height ($\bar{y}$) is the average height of the ramp above the ground. \\ The steepness of the ramp (slope) does not depend on whether the ramp is built on flat ground ($\bar{y}$ is low) or on top of a large pedestal ($\bar{y}$ is high). The two properties are independent concepts, and the $Cov(\bar{y}, \hat{\beta}_1)=0$ result confirms their statistical independence. Because $\hat{\beta}_1$ is only concerned with the rotation (relative change), and $\bar{y}$ is only concerned with the vertical position (average level), they are effectively isolated

questions.questionText: True or False: The two hyperplane classifiers $ \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + b $ and $ \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{x} + q $ with $ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2 $, $ b, q \in \mathbb{R} $ have the same decision boundary if $ \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0} $ and $ b + q = 0 $. Give a brief proof if your answer is T, else give a concrete counter example if your answer is F.
questions.questionHtml:
True or False:

The two hyperplane classifiers $ \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + b $ and $ \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{x} + q $ with $ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2 $, $ b, q \in \mathbb{R} $ have the same decision boundary if $ \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0} $ and $ b + q = 0 $. Give a brief proof if your answer is T, else give a concrete counter example if your answer is F.
questions.explanation: Two hyperplanes \( \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + b = 0 \) and \( \mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{x} + q = 0 \) define the same decision boundary if they are scalar multiples of each other. That is, there exists \( k \neq 0 \) such that: \[ \mathbf{p} = k \mathbf{a}, \quad q = k b. \] If we take  \( k = 2 \): \[ \mathbf{p} = 2\mathbf{a}, \quad q = 2b. \] Then the decision boundary is: \[ 2\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + 2b = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{x} + b = 0 \] Counterexample: Let \( \mathbf{a} = [1, 0]^T \), \( b = 0 \), and \( \mathbf{p} = [2, 0]^T \), \( q = 0 \). - First classifier: \( 1 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 = 0 \) → \( x_1 = 0 \). - Second classifier: \( 2 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 = 0 \) → \( x_1 = 0 \). So they have the same decision boundary (the y-axis), but \( \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{p} = [3,0]^T \neq 0 \) and \( b + q = 0 \). Thus, the condition is not satisfied. Final Answer: False.  soudipta_dutta answered Sep 21, 2025 • edited Sep 21, 2025 by

There exists a unique feature map $\phi_{\text{lin}}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^D$ for the linear kernel such that 
\[
\langle \phi_{\text{lin}}(\mathbf{x}), \phi_{\text{lin}}(\mathbf{y}) \rangle = \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle

questions.explanation: Linear kernel $\Rightarrow K(x,y) = x^T y$ One feature map is identity map: $\Rightarrow \phi(x) = x$. Here, \[ \phi(x)^T \phi(y) = x^T y \] Analysis: 2 maps that yield the Same Kernel Value $\Rightarrow$ Preservation of dot products $\Rightarrow$ Orthogonal transformations (rotations & reflections) where $ Q^T Q = I $ Let a new feature map be: \[ \phi_1(x) = Qx \] Then \[ \phi_1(x)^T \phi_1(y) = x^T Q^T Q y = x^T y \quad \text{(yields the same kernel)} \] But we can have an infinite number of orthogonal matrices (rotation & reflection matrices by any angle). Hence, we can have an infinite number of feature maps that all produce the same kernel. $\Rightarrow$ Feature map is NOT unique soudipta_dutta answered Sep 19, 2025 • edited Sep 19, 2025 by soudipta_dutta soudipta_dutta comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: \[ \lambda^2 - \mathrm{trace}(P)\lambda + \det(P) = 0 \] \[ \lambda^2 - 1\lambda + (-6) = 0 \] \[ (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 2) = 0 \] So, the eigenvalues are $ \lambda_1 = 3 $ and $ \lambda_2 = -2 $. \[ \mathrm{trace}(P^n) = \lambda_1^n + \lambda_2^n \] \[ \mathrm{trace}(P^3) = \lambda_1^3 + \lambda_2^3 = 3^3 + (-2)^3 = 27 + (-8) = 19 \] \[ \mathrm{trace}(P^4) = \lambda_1^4 + \lambda_2^4 = 3^4 + (-2)^4 = 81 + 16 = 97 \] \[ \mathrm{trace}(P^4 - P^3) = \mathrm{trace}(P^4) - \mathrm{trace}(P^3) \] \[ \mathrm{trace}(P^4 - P^3) = 97 - 19 = 78 \] soudipta_dutta answered Sep 9, 2025 • edited Sep 9, 2025 by soudipta_dutta soudipta_dutta comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionText: The possible set of eigenvalues of a $ 4 \times 4 $ skew-symmetric orthogonal real matrix is    (A) $ \{\pm i\} $    (B) $ \{\pm i, \pm 1\} $    (C) $ \{\pm 1\} $    (D) $ \{0, \pm i\} $
questions.questionHtml:
The possible set of eigenvalues of a $ 4 \times 4 $ skew-symmetric orthogonal real matrix is

   (A) $ \{\pm i\} $
   (B) $ \{\pm i, \pm 1\} $
   (C) $ \{\pm 1\} $
   (D) $ \{0, \pm i\} $
questions.explanation: Combine the Properties : Since \(A\) is orthogonal: \(A^T = A^{-1}\).   But \(A\) is skew-symmetric: \(A^T = -A\).   So, \(-A = A^{-1}\) ⟹ \(A^{-1} = -A\)  ⟹ Multiplying both sides by \(A\): \(I = -A^2\) ⟹ \(A^2 = -I\).  Find the Eigenvalues :  Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of \(A\). Then: $$ A^2 = -I \implies A^2 v = -v \implies \lambda^2 v = -v$$ $$ \implies \lambda^2 = -1 \implies \lambda = \pm i. $$ So, the eigenvalues are purely imaginary: \(i\) and \(-i\). Correct Option: \[ \boxed{A} \] One more thing :  0 cannot occur because orthogonality implies invertibility (no zero eigenvalue).

questions.questionHtml:
Let $M$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. We define an elementary row operation on $M$ to be one of the following:

  1. Interchanging some two rows of $M$.
  2. Multiplying a row in $M$ by a non-zero scalar.
  3. Adding a scalar multiple of one row of $M$ to another row of $M$.

An $n \times n$ matrix is said to be elementary if it is the result of a single elementary row operation performed on the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

Which of the following statements is/are true? Justify your answer with a short proof, if the statement is true, otherwise, provide a counterexample.

An elementary row operation on a $n \times n$ matrix $A$ results in a matrix with the same determinant as that of $A.$

options.text: Multiplying a row in $M$ by a non-zero scalar.

options.label: C
options.text: Adding a scalar multiple of one row of $M$ to another row of $M$.

questions.explanation: Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{(the $2 \times 2$ identity matrix).} \] \[ \det(A) = (1)(1) - (0)(0) = 1. \] Swap rows: \[ A' = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det(A') = (0)(0) - (1)(1) = -1. \] Since $\det(A') = -1 \ne \det(A) = 1$, the statement is false. Let \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det(A) = 1. \] Perform the row operation $ R_1 \to 5R_1 $: \[ A'' = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \det(A'') = (5)(1) - (0)(0) = 5. \] Since $\det(A'') = 5 \ne \det(A) = 1$, the statement is false. Adding a scalar multiple of one row to another: Effect on Determinant: This operation does not change the determinant. Correct Answer : \[ \boxed{C} \]

questions.explanation: Cayley Transform : Mapping Between Anti-symmetric and Orthogonal Matrices Forward Transform: The standard transform maps an Anti-symmetric matrix ($A$) to an orthogonal matrix ($Q$). The formula is: $$ Q=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1} $$ This is the fundamental relationship. Inverse Transform: The inverse transform maps an orthogonal matrix ($Q$) back to an Anti-symmetric matrix ($A$), with the condition that $-1$ is not an eigenvalue of $Q$. This immediately tells us that if $A$ is anti-symmetric, $Q$ must be orthogonal. The formula for this inverse is: $$ A=(I-Q)(I+Q)^{-1} $$ Definitions :   Anti-symmetric matrix ($A$): A square matrix where the transpose is equal to the negative of the matrix ($A^T=-A$).   Orthogonal matrix ($Q$): A square matrix where the transpose is equal to its inverse ($Q^T=Q^{-1}$ or $Q^TQ=I$). questions.explanation: For $n \times n$ real symmetric matrices:  $n$ diagonal elements. $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ off-diagonal elements (upper triangle). So, total dimension $= n + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ Base dimension $= \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ If you impose:      Trace zero: subtract 1 (independent).      Sum of off-diagonals zero: subtract 1 (independent). So, dimension $= \frac{n(n+1)}{2} - 2$ For $n=7$: $\frac{7 \cdot 8}{2} - 2 = 28 - 2 = 26$ The correct option is D. REMEMBER :  The base dimension of an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix is $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.  For an $n \times n$ skew-symmetric matrix, the dimension is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.  For a general $m \times n$ matrix, the dimension is $mn$.

We can find a vector $x$ such that $x^t x=1$, where $t$ denotes the transpose, and     (A) $x^t Ax > \lambda_1$     (B) $x^t Ax < \lambda_n$     (C) $\lambda_n \le x^t Ax \le \lambda_1$     (D) $x^t Ax > n\alpha$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ positive semi-definite matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n$, and with $\alpha$ as the maximum diagonal entry. We can find a vector $x$ such that $x^t x=1$, where $t$ denotes the transpose, and

    (A) $x^t Ax > \lambda_1$
    (B) $x^t Ax < \lambda_n$
    (C) $\lambda_n \le x^t Ax \le \lambda_1$
    (D) $x^t Ax > n\alpha$
questions.explanation: The problem states that \[ x^{\top}x = 1. \] This property is a direct result of the Rayleigh quotient theorem.   The Rayleigh quotient for a matrix \(A\) and a non-zero vector \(x\) is defined as \[ R(x) = \frac{x^{\top}Ax}{x^{\top}x}. \] All positive semi-definite matrices are symmetric matrices.   Since \(x^{\top}x = 1\), the vector \(x\) is a unit vector.   Then the Rayleigh quotient simplifies to \[ R(x) = x^{\top}Ax. \] The theorem states that for any unit vector \(x\), \[ \lambda_{\min} \;\leq\; x^{\top}Ax \;\leq\; \lambda_{\max}, \] which implies \[ \lambda_{n} \;\leq\; x^{\top}Ax \;\leq\; \lambda_{1}. \] \[ \text{Therefore, Option C is the correct answer.} \]

questions.explanation: Magic Trio Vectors The "Magic Trio" vectors are: \[ (1,0), \quad (0,1), \quad (1,1) \] These vectors are pairwise independent but as a set they are linearly dependent. Let the vectors be: \[ x_1 = (1,0), \quad x_2 = (0,1), \quad x_3 = (1,1). \] Properties of these vectors:      $m = 3$ and $d = 2$.      Any pair of these vectors is linearly independent.      The set of all three vectors is linearly dependent, because:     \[ (1,0) + (0,1) - (1,1) = (0,0). \] This set of three vectors forms a clique of size 3 in a $d=2$ space. Counter Example To show that the degree of a vertex can exceed the dimension $d$, we use a counterexample in $d=2$ ($\mathbb{R}^2$) for visualization.      Start with a vector $v_1 = (1,0)$.      Add $v_2 = (0,1)$. It is not collinear with $v_1$, so an edge exists between them.      Add $v_3 = (1,1)$. It is not collinear with $v_1$, so an edge exists.

No.  Hence , Disconnected.  Orthogonal Matrices :  $$ A^T A = I $$ Here $\det(A) = \pm 1$ 2D rotations (det +1) vs. reflections (det -1).  Can you smoothly change a rotation into a reflection? No. Passing through det  =  0 isn't allowed for orthogonal matrices. Hence , Disconnected. Trace-Zero Matrices  { A ∣ t r ( A ) = 0 } : Let me ask a question : Can you pick 2 metrices A and B where Trace(A)  = Trace(B) = 0 ?? Answer is YES.  Now,the main Question : Can you draw a Straight Line , a Path, tA + (1 - t)B, between them ??  YES. Let $\mathbf{w}=A \mathbf{v}$, and suppose $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B$ corresponding to eigenvalue 5, i.e., $B \mathbf{w}=5 \mathbf{w}$. Which of the following statements are correct? $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B^{2}$ with eigenvalue $25$. $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $B A$ with eigenvalue $-15$. $\mathbf{v}$ is not necessarily an eigenvector of $A B$. $\mathbf{w}$ is always an eigenvector of $A B$ with eigenvalue $-15$.
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two $5 \times 5$ matrices. Suppose $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to eigenvalue -3 , i.e., $A \mathbf{v}=-3 \mathbf{v}$. Let $\mathbf{w}=A \mathbf{v}$, and suppose $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B$ corresponding to eigenvalue 5, i.e., $B \mathbf{w}=5 \mathbf{w}$.
Which of the following statements are correct?

  1. $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B^{2}$ with eigenvalue $25$.
     
  2. $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $B A$ with eigenvalue $-15$.
     
  3. $\mathbf{v}$ is not necessarily an eigenvector of $A B$.
     
  4. $\mathbf{w}$ is always an eigenvector of $A B$ with eigenvalue $-15$.

options.label: A
options.text: $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B^{2}$ with eigenvalue $25$.

options.label: B
options.text: $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $B A$ with eigenvalue $-15$.

options.label: C
options.text: $\mathbf{v}$ is not necessarily an eigenvector of $A B$.

options.label: D
options.text: $\mathbf{w}$ is always an eigenvector of $A B$ with eigenvalue $-15$.

questions.explanation: A: Since $B \mathbf{w}=5 \mathbf{w}$, then $B^{2} \mathbf{w}=B(5 \mathbf{w})=25 \mathbf{w}$, so $\mathbf{w}$ is an eigenvector of $B^{2}$. B: $\mathbf{w}=-3 \mathbf{v}$, and $B \mathbf{w}=5 \mathbf{w}=-15 \mathbf{v}$, hence $B A \mathbf{v}=-15 \mathbf{v}$, so $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $B A$. C: $\mathbf{C}$ : We cannot conclude $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A B$, since we don't know $B \mathbf{v}$. D : $A B \mathbf{w}$ is not defined unless we know how $A$ acts on $\mathbf{w}$; also, $\mathbf{w}$ is not generally guaranteed to be an eigenvector of $A B$ . questions.questionText: Let $B$ be a $10 \times 10$ matrix in which all entries are 1. Then $B$ has two eigenvalues:  10 (with multiplicity 1 )   0 (with multiplicity 9 ) Now define a matrix $A=\left(a_{i j}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{10 \times 10}$ as follows: $$ a_{i j}= \begin{cases}1 & \text { if } i \neq j \\ \alpha+1 & \text { if } i=j\end{cases} $$ where $\alpha>0$. Let $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote the largest and smallest eigenvalues of matrix $A$, respectively. If it is given that: $$ \lambda+\mu=24 $$ then the value of $\alpha$ is: $6$ $7$ $8$ $10$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $B$ be a $10 \times 10$ matrix in which all entries are 1.
Then $B$ has two eigenvalues:

  •  10 (with multiplicity 1 )
  •   0 (with multiplicity 9 )

Now define a matrix $A=\left(a_{i j}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{10 \times 10}$ as follows:
$$
a_{i j}= \begin{cases}1 & \text { if } i \neq j \\ \alpha+1 & \text { if } i=j\end{cases}
$$
where $\alpha>0$.
Let $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote the largest and smallest eigenvalues of matrix $A$, respectively. If it is given that:
$$
\lambda+\mu=24
$$
then the value of $\alpha$ is:

  1. $6$
  2. $7$
  3. $8$
  4. $10$
questions.explanation: We can write the matrix $A$ as: $$ A=B+\alpha I $$ Eigenvalues of $A$ are the eigenvalues of $B$ shifted by $\alpha$. So the eigenvalues of $A$ are: - $10+\alpha$ (once) - $\alpha$ (nine times) Hence, $$ \lambda=10+\alpha, \quad \mu=\alpha $$ Given: $$ \lambda+\mu=24 \Rightarrow(10+\alpha)+\alpha=24 \Rightarrow 10+2 \alpha=24 $$ Solving: $$ 2 \alpha=14 \Rightarrow \alpha=7 $$ Correct answer: B. 7

questions.explanation: Analysis of Inverse Matrix Entries Let \( A = [a_{ij}] \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times n} \) be a square matrix with integer entries, and suppose \( AB = I \), i.e., \( B = A^{-1} \). We're analyzing under what conditions the entries \( b_{ij} \) of \( B \) are also integers. If \( \det(A) = 1 \), then \( \det(B) = 1 \) From the equation \( AB = I \), take determinants: $$ \det(AB) = \det(A)\cdot\det(B) = \det(I) = 1 \\ \Rightarrow \det(B) = \frac{1}{\det(A)} = 1 $$ This holds if \( \det(A) = 1 \). Hence, the statement is true . A sufficient condition for each \( b_{ij} \) to be an integer is that \( \det(A) \) is an integer This is false . Counterexample: $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \det(A) = 4, \quad A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} $$ Even though \( \det(A) \in \mathbb{Z} \), the inverse contains fractions. So having an integer determinant is not sufficient to ensure integer entries in the inverse. \(

questions.questionText: Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, A \neq I_{n}$, and suppose $A^{2}=A$. Which of the following statements is false? $\left(I_{n}-A\right)^{2}=I_{n}-A$ $\operatorname{Tr}(A)=\operatorname{Rank}(A)$ $\operatorname{Rank}(A)+\operatorname{Rank}\left(I_{n}-A\right)=n$ All eigenvalues of $A$ are equal to 1
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, A \neq I_{n}$, and suppose $A^{2}=A$. Which of the following statements is false?

  1. $\left(I_{n}-A\right)^{2}=I_{n}-A$
     
  2. $\operatorname{Tr}(A)=\operatorname{Rank}(A)$
     
  3. $\operatorname{Rank}(A)+\operatorname{Rank}\left(I_{n}-A\right)=n$
     
  4. All eigenvalues of $A$ are equal to 1

options.label: D
options.text: All eigenvalues of $A$ are equal to 1

questions.explanation: Since $A^{2}=A$, matrix $A$ is idempotent.  The eigenvalues of $A$ satisfy $\lambda^{2}=\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda \in\{0,1\}$.  Hence, not all eigenvalues are necessarily 1 . So, $\mathbf{D}$ is false. A. True: Let $B=I_{n}-A$. Then: $$ B^{2}=\left(I_{n}-A\right)^{2}=I_{n}-2 A+A^{2}=I_{n}-2 A+A=I_{n}-A=B $$ So $B^{2}=B$, hence $\mathbf{A}$ is true. B. True: Since eigenvalues of $A$ are 0 or 1, the trace (sum of eigenvalues) equals the number of 1's, which also equals the rank (number of linearly independent columns). $$ \operatorname{Tr}(A)=\operatorname{Rank}(A) $$ C. True: Let $r=\operatorname{Rank}(A)$. Then the nullity of $A$ is $n-r$. Note that $\operatorname{ker}(A)=\operatorname{Im}\left(I_{n}-A\right)$, so: $$ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Rank}\left(I_{n}-A\right)=\operatorname{dim}\left(\operatorname{Im}\left(I_{n}-A\right)\right)=\operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{ker}(A))=n-r \\ \Rightarrow \operatorname{Rank}(A)+\operatorname{Rank}\left(I_{n}-A\right)=n \end{ga

However, they do share the same non-zero eigenvalues (with multiplicities). The remaining eigenvalues are zero, added as needed according to the size of the matrix. questions.questionText: Let $\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3$ be three linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Apply the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process to obtain an orthogonal basis $\left\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\right\}$. For any vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is defined as: $$ \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{b}} \mathbf{a}=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \mathbf{b} $$ Which of the following correctly applies the Gram-Schmidt process? $$ \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_2, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_2} \mathbf{u}_3 $$ $$ \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2+2 \mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3+\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_3+\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_2} \mathbf{u}_3 $$ $$ \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_2, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_2} \mathbf{u}_3 $$ $$ \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_3-\mathbf{u}_2 $$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3$ be three linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Apply the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process to obtain an orthogonal basis $\left\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\right\}$.
For any vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is defined as:
$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{b}} \mathbf{a}=\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \mathbf{b}
$$

Which of the following correctly applies the Gram-Schmidt process?


  1. $$
    \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_2, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_2} \mathbf{u}_3
    $$

  2. $$
    \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2+2 \mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3+\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_3+\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_2} \mathbf{u}_3
    $$

  3. $$
    \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_2, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_2} \mathbf{u}_3
    $$

  4. $$
    \mathbf{v}_1=\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_1} \mathbf{u}_3-\mathbf{u}_2
    $$
questions.explanation: The Gram-Schmidt process generates an orthogonal basis from a given basis as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}_1 & =\mathbf{u}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_2 & =\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\frac{\mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{v}_1 \\ \mathbf{v}_3 & =\mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{u}_3-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{v}_2} \mathbf{u}_3 \\ & =\mathbf{u}_3-\frac{\mathbf{u}_3 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1}{\mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1} \mathbf{v}_1-\frac{\mathbf{u}_3 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2}{\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2} \mathbf{v}_2 \end{aligned} $$ GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Minimum: $0$ , Maximum: $5$ Minimum: $2$, Maximum: $5$ Minimum: $3$ , Maximum: $4$ Minimum: $0$ , Maximum: $2$
questions.questionHtml:
Let $T: \mathbb{R}^5 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ be a linear transformation.
Which of the following are the minimum and maximum possible dimensions of the null space of $T$ ?

  1. Minimum: $0$ , Maximum: $5$
  2. Minimum: $2$, Maximum: $5$
  3. Minimum: $3$ , Maximum: $4$
  4. Minimum: $0$ , Maximum: $2$
questions.explanation: By the Rank-Nullity Theorem: $$ \operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{domain})=\operatorname{rank}+\operatorname{nullity} \Rightarrow 5=\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T) $$ Maximum rank $=\min (5,3)=3 \Rightarrow$ nullity $=5-3=2$ Minimum rank $=0 \Rightarrow$ nullity $=5-0=5$ Thus, the null space of $T$ can have dimension from $2$ to $5$. What is the coordinate vector of $\mathbf{v}$ with respect to the new basis $\mathcal{C}$ ? $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2\end{array}\right]^T$ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & 0\end{array}\right]^T$ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 2\end{array}\right]^T$ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1\end{array}\right]^T$

$$

Now consider a new basis $\mathcal{C}=\left\{\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_1+2 \mathbf{b}_2\right\}$. What is the coordinate vector of $\mathbf{v}$ with respect to the new basis $\mathcal{C}$ ?

  1. $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2\end{array}\right]^T$
  2. $\left[\begin{array}{ll}2 & 0\end{array}\right]^T$
  3. $\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 2\end{array}\right]^T$

We want to write $\mathbf{v}$ as: $$ \mathbf{v}=x \cdot \mathbf{b}_1+y \cdot\left(\mathbf{b}_1+2 \mathbf{b}_2\right)=(x+y) \mathbf{b}_1+2 y \mathbf{b}_2 $$ Matching this with $2 \mathbf{b}_1+4 \mathbf{b}_2$, we get: $$ x+y=2, \quad 2 y=4 \Rightarrow y=2, x=0 $$ So in basis $\mathcal{C}$, the coordinate vector is: $$ [\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 2 \end{array}\right]^T $$ GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation: To check positive definiteness, test whether all leading principal minors are positive: First minor: $3>0$ Second leading principal minor: $$ \operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{cc} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{array}\right]=3(2)-(-1)(-1)=6-1=5>0 $$ Third (full) determinant: $$ \operatorname{det} A=3\left(2 \cdot 3-(-1)^2\right)+1(-1 \cdot 3-(-1) \cdot 0)=3(6-1)=15>0 $$ All leading principal minors are positive $\Rightarrow$ Matrix is positive definite. questions.questionHtml:
Consider the matrix
$$
A(x)=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
1+x^2 & 7 & 11 \\
3 x & 2 x & 4 \\
8 x & 17 & 13
\end{array}\right], \quad x \in \mathbb{R}
$$

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. $A(x)$ has eigenvalue $0$ for some $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A(x)$ for any $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $A(x)$ has eigenvalue $0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  4. $A(x)$ is invertible for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$

options.label: B
options.text: $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A(x)$ for any $x \in \mathbb{R}$

questions.explanation: Let us consider the eigenvalue $0$ . That means checking when the matrix $A(x)$ becomes non-invertible, i.e., when $\operatorname{det}(A(x))=0$. Compute the determinant: $$ \operatorname{det}(A(x))=\left(1+x^2\right) \cdot(2 x \cdot 13-4 \cdot 17)-7 \cdot(3 x \cdot 13-4 \cdot 8 x)+11 \cdot(3 x \cdot 17-2 x \cdot 8 x) $$ This is a polynomial in $x$, so it can have real roots, i.e., values of $x$ for which the determinant is 0 . Hence, for some $x \in \mathbb{R}, A(x)$ has eigenvalue 0 . Option B is false because we just showed that 0 can be an eigenvalue. Option C is false because 0 is not an eigenvalue for all $x$, only some. Option D is false because $A(x)$ is not invertible for all $x$, as the determinant can be zero for some $x$. So the only correct answer is A.

questions.explanation: Since the system is homogeneous and has infinitely many solutions, it must have non-trivial solutions, which implies that the nullity of $A \geq 1$. Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem: $$ \operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A)=3 $$ So, rank must be at most 2 . Hence, possible values of rank are: $$ 0,1,2 $$ GO Classes answered Jul 20, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.explanation:
The rank of a matrix is the number of non-zero rows in its row echelon form. For an upper triangular matrix, each non-zero pivot (i.e., leading diagonal entry) contributes to the rank. Let's analyze each case: (i) $\alpha=0,  eta=\gamma 
eq 0$ Row 3 becomes $[000  eta]$ and row 4 is $[000 \gamma]$. Since $ eta=\gamma 
eq 0$, row 3 still has a non-zero entry (in column 4), and so does row 4. Hence, we still have all 4 non-zero rows. Rank $=4 \geq 3 ightarrow$ Valid (ii) $\alpha= eta=\gamma=0$ Then rows 3 and 4 become all zero. Only rows 1 and 2 remain non-zero. Rank $=2<3 ightarrow$ Not valid (iii) $ eta=\gamma=0, \alpha 
eq 0$ Row 3 is $[00 \alpha 0]$, which is non-zero, and row 4 is zero. We have 3 non-zero rows. Rank $=3 \geq 3 ightarrow$ Valid (iv) $\alpha= eta=\gamma 
eq 0$ Then all diagonal entries are non-zero, so all rows are non-zero. Rank $=4 \geq 3 ightarrow$ Valid GO Classes answered Jul 5, 2025 • reshown Jul 7, 2025 by GO Classes Support GO C

questions.questionHtml:
Let $V$ be a vector space with $\operatorname{dim}(V)=5$.
Let $W$ and $Z$ be subspaces of $V$ such that
$$
\operatorname{dim}(W)=3, \quad \operatorname{dim}(Z)=4 .
$$
Which of the following are possible values of $\operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)$ ?

  1. $0$
     
  2. $1$
     
  3. $2$
     
  4. $3$
questions.explanation: Answer: C,D 1. If $W$ is completely contained in $Z$, then the entire 3 -dimensional $W$ lies inside $Z$. So, $$ \operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)=\operatorname{dim}(W)=3 $$ 2. Now think of the minimum possible overlap. $W$ and $Z$ together try to span $3+4=7$ dimensions, but the ambient space $V$ has only 5 dimensions. This means they must overlap by at least $7-5=2$ dimensions. So, the smallest possible value is $$ \operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)=2 $$ Therefore, the possible values of $$ \operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z) $$ are: 2 and 3. We place 5 basis vectors (A to E) in a row and visually represent which vectors are included in $W$ and $Z$. Case 1 : Minimum Intersection $(\operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)=2)$ Case 2 : Maximum Intersection $(\operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)=3$ ) Overlap: Points C, D, E are common $\operatorname{dim}(W \cap Z)=3$ GO Classes answered Jun 29, 2025 • edited Jun 29, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment.

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be a real symmetric matrix whose only eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$ .

What is the rank of the matrix $A$ ?

  2. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$
  3. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=0$
  4. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$
questions.explanation: Answer : B Since $A$ is real symmetric, it is diagonalizable. So we have: $$ \operatorname{GM}(\lambda)=\operatorname{AM}(\lambda) \quad \text { for each eigenvalue } \lambda $$ Given: null space of $A-I$ has dimension $m$, i.e., geometric multiplicity of eigenvalue 1 is $m$, and hence algebraic multiplicity of eigenvalue $1$ is also $m$. The only eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$ . Since the total degree of the characteristic polynomial is $n$, the multiplicity of eigenvalue $0$ is $n-m$. So, the number of nonzero eigenvalues ($1$) $=m$ Hence, $$ \operatorname{rank}(A)=\text { number of nonzero eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity) }=m $$ Also, we can easily write the characteristic polynomial as: $$ (\lambda-1)^{m} \cdot \lambda^{n-m} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 29, 2025 • edited Jul 2, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $A$ be a singular $N \times N$ matrix with real entries, and let $\mathbf{b}$ be an $N \times 1$ column vector. Let $A^{\mathrm{T}}$ and $\mathbf{b}^{\mathrm{T}}$ denote their transposes. Consider the system of equations:
$$
A^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}
$$
The system has a solution if and only if $\mathbf{b}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{u}=0$ for all column vectors $\mathbf{u}$ such that:
  1. $A \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$
  2. $A^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$
  3. $A \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{b}$
  4. $A^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{b}^{\mathrm{T}}$
questions.explanation: Explanation We are given the system: $$ A^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} $$ This implies that $\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{col}\left(A^{\mathrm{T}}\right)$, and since the column space of $A^{\mathrm{T}}$ is the same as the row space of $A$, we have: $$ \mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{row}(A) $$ Now, from linear algebra, we know: $$ \operatorname{row}(A) \perp \operatorname{null}(A) $$ That is, every vector in the row space of $A$ is orthogonal to every vector in the null space of $A$. So, for the system $A^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ to be consistent, the vector $\mathbf{b}$ must be orthogonal to every vector $\mathbf{u}$ in $\operatorname{null}(A)$. In other words, $$ \mathbf{b}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{u}=0 \quad \text { for all } \mathbf{u} \text { such that } A \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 29, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ be subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ defined as:
$$
W_{1}=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^{3} \mid x+y+z=0\right\}, \quad W_{2}=\left\{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^{3} \mid x-y+z=0\right\}
$$
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{3}$ be a subspace such that:

  • (i) $W \cap W_{2}=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,1)\}$
  • (ii) $W \cap W_{1}$ is orthogonal to $W \cap W_{2}$ (with respect to the standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ )


Which of the following is the correct description of $W$ ?

  1. $\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,-1),(0,1,1)\}$
  2. $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,-1),(0,1,-1)\}$
  3. $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,-1),(0,1,1)\}$
  4. $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,-1),(1,0,1)\}$
questions.explanation: Answer: A We are given: $W \cap W_{2}=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,1)\}$ $W \cap W_{1} \perp W \cap W_{2}$ Let $v_{1}=(0,1,1) \in W \cap W_{2}$ Let $v_{2}=(x, y, z) \in W \cap W_{1}$, so: $x+y+z=0 \quad\left(\right.$ from $\left.W_{1}\right)$ $\left\langle v_{1}, v_{2}\right\rangle=y+z=0 \Rightarrow z=-y$ From above: $x+y+(-y)=0 \Rightarrow x=0$ So, $v_{2}=(0, y,-y)=y \cdot(0,1,-1) \Rightarrow W \cap W_{1}=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,-1)\}$ Hence, $$ W=\operatorname{span}\{(0,1,-1),(0,1,1)\} $$ GO Classes answered Jun 29, 2025 • edited Jul 2, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. questions.questionHtml:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be a real matrix with rank $r$.
Suppose the linear system $A x=b$ has a solution for every $b \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$.
Then which of the following statements is/are necessarily true?

  1. $m=r$
  2. The column space of $A$ is a proper subspace
    of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
  3. The null space of $A$ is a nontrivial subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whenever $m=n$
  4. If $m \geq n$, then $m=n$

options.label: B
options.text: The column space of $A$ is a proper subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$

options.label: C
options.text: The null space of $A$ is a nontrivial subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whenever $m=n$

questions.explanation: Answer: A,D We are given that the system $A x=b$ has a solution for every $b \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. This means the column space of $A$ must span the entire $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ : $$ \operatorname{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^{m} \Rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{Col}(A))=m \Rightarrow r=m $$ $m=r$ This follows directly from the above observation. True The column space of $A$ is a proper subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ Since $\operatorname{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^{m}$, it is not a proper subspace. False The null space of $A$ is a nontrivial subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whenever $m=n$ If $m=n$, and $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m=n$, then by the rank-nullity theorem: $$ \operatorname{nullity}(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)=n-n=0 $$ So the null space is trivial. False If $m \geq n$, then $m=n$ Since $\operatorname{rank}(A)=m$ and $\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \min (m, n)$, we must have: $$ m \leq n $$ So if $m \geq n$ and $m \leq n$, it follows that $m=n$. True GO Classes answered Jun 29

$$
N(A)=\left\{(x, y, z, \omega) \in \mathbb{R}^{4} \mid x+y+z=0, x+y+\omega=0\right\}
$$
Which of the following statements is/are true?
  1. $\operatorname{dim}($ Column space of $A)=1$
  2. $\operatorname{dim}($ Column space of $A)=2$

questions.explanation: Answer: B Explanation: We are given a null space defined by two linear equations: $$ x+y+z=0 \quad \text { and } \quad x+y+\omega=0 $$ Subtracting the two equations: $$ (x+y+\omega)-(x+y+z)=\omega-z=0 \Rightarrow \omega=z $$ Substitute $\omega=z$ into the system. The only constraint becomes: $$ x+y+z=0 \quad \text { and } \quad \omega=z $$ Let $y=s$ and $z=t$. Then: $$ x=-y-z=-s-t, \quad \omega=z=t $$ So any vector in the null space can be written as: $$ (x, y, z, \omega)=(-s-t, s, t, t)=s(-1,1,0,0)+t(-1,0,1,1) $$ This shows that the null space is 2 -dimensional and spanned by the vectors: $$ v_{1}=(-1,1,0,0), \quad v_{2}=(-1,0,1,1) $$ Therefore, $\operatorname{dim}(N(A))=2$. Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem for $A \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}$, we have: $$ \operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{dim}(N(A))=4 \Rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(A)=4-2=2 $$ So, the dimension of the column space of $A$ is also 2 . Now, verify whether the given set $S=\{(1,1,1,0),(1,1,0,1)\}$ is in the null space.

Which of the following real quadratic forms on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is positive definite?
  1. $Q(x, y)=x y$
  2. $Q(x, y)=x^{2}-x y+y^{2}$
  3. $Q(x, y)=x^{2}+2 x y+y^{2}$
  4. $Q(x, y)=x^{2}+x y$
questions.explanation: Answer: B A real quadratic form $Q(x, y)$ is positive definite if: $$ Q(x, y)>0 \quad \text { for all }(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2} \backslash\{(0,0)\} $$ This means: $Q(x, y)$ is always strictly positive unless both $x=0$ and $y=0$. Option B , $$ Q(x, y)=x^{2}-x y+y^{2}, $$ is the only positive definite quadratic form, since $$ Q(x, y)>0 \quad \text { for all }(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2} \backslash\{(0,0)\} . $$ The other forms take zero or negative values for some nonzero inputs. A. $Q(x, y)=x y$ Try $(x, y)=(1,1) \Rightarrow Q=1$ and $(x, y)=(-1,1) \Rightarrow Q=-1$. Since $Q$ takes both positive and negative values, it is not positive definite. B . $Q(x, y)=x^{2}-x y+y^{2}$ Rewrite the expression: $$ Q(x, y)=x^{2}-x y+y^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(x-y)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right) $$ which is a sum of squares, hence $Q(x, y)>0$ for all $(x, y) \neq(0,0)$. questions.explanation: Answer: A,B,C Explanation: Let the eigenvalues of $A$ be $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \lambda_{3}, \lambda_{4} \in \mathbb{R}$. Since $A$ is symmetric, it is diagonalizable with real eigenvalues, and since $A$ is non-singular, none of the eigenvalues are zero: $\lambda_{i} \neq 0 \forall i$. A. The eigenvalues of $p I+A$ are $\lambda_{i}+p$. For sufficiently large $p$, all $\lambda_{i}+p>0$, so the matrix becomes positive definite. This statement is true. B. The eigenvalues of $A^{p}$ are $\lambda_{i}^{p}$. If some $\lambda_{i}<0$, then: $-\lambda_{i}^{p}<0$ if $p$ is odd $-\lambda_{i}^{p}>0$ if $p$ is even Hence, for even $p$, all eigenvalues are positive. This statement is true. $\mathbf{C}$. The eigenvalues of $A^{-p}$ are $\lambda_{i}^{-p}$. If we choose $p$ to be even, then $\lambda_{i}^{-p}>0$ for all $\lambda_{i} \neq 0$, which they are by assumption. This statement is true. D. Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix with real entries. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\operatorname{rank}\left(A^{T} A\right) \leq \operatorname{rank}(A)$
     
  2. $\operatorname{rank}\left(A^{T} A\right)=\operatorname{rank}(A)$
     
  3. $\operatorname{rank}\left(A^{T} A\right)>\operatorname{rank}(A)$
     
  4. $\operatorname{rank}\left(A^{T} A\right) \leq \min (m, n)$
questions.explanation: Fact: $$ \operatorname{nullity}\left(A^{T} A\right)=\operatorname{nullity}(A) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \operatorname{rank} \text { of } A^{T} A=\operatorname{rank} \text { of } A $$ A.The rank of the matrix $A^{T} A$ is less than or equal to the rank of the matrix $A$ True - This always holds for matrix products in general. In this case, equality also holds. B.The rank of the matrix $A^{T} A$ is equal to the rank of the matrix $A$ True - Follows directly from the fact stated above. C.The rank of the matrix $A^{T} A$ is greater than the rank of the matrix $A$ False - The rank of $A^{T} A$ can never exceed the rank of $A$. D.The rank of the matrix $A^{T} A$ is less than or equal to $\min (m, n)$ True - Since $\operatorname{rank}\left(A^{T} A\right)=\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \min (m, n)$, this always holds. The entries become: $$ A_{3}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1-1 & 1-2 & 1-3 \\ 2-1 & 2-2 & 2-3 \\ 3-1 & 3-2 & 3-3 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 0 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array}\right] $$ Looking closely at the rows: $$ R_{1}=[0,-1,-2], \quad R_{2}=[1,0,-1], \quad R_{3}=[2,1,0] $$ We notice that each row is increasing by a fixed amount compared to the previous one. So, all the rows lie in the span of just two vectors: the first row $R_{1}$, and the all-ones vector. questions.explanation: We are given: $$ P^{2}=P $$ This implies that $P$ is an idempotent matrix, i.e., applying it twice is the same as applying it once. Idempotent matrices have special spectral properties. Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $P$, and $v \neq 0$ be its corresponding eigenvector. Then: $$ P^{2} v=P v \Rightarrow \lambda^{2} v=\lambda v \Rightarrow\left(\lambda^{2}-\lambda\right) v=0 \Rightarrow \lambda(\lambda-1)=0 $$ So the only possible eigenvalues of $P$ are 0 and 1 . Since $P$ is diagonalizable (being idempotent with real eigenvalues), it is similar to a diagonal matrix with $0$ s and $1$ s on the diagonal. Possible diagonal matrices similar to $P$ include: $$ \left[\begin{array}{ll} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right], \quad\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right], \quad\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] $$ In each case: The trace of $P$ is the sum of the diagonal entries, i.e., the sum of eigenvalues. Let $A$ be a $5 \times 5$ matrix, and suppose that the dimension of the solution space of the homogeneous system $A x=0$ is at least $2$ .

questions.explanation: We are given: Number of linearly independent solutions of $A x=0 \geq 2$ The dimension of the solution space of $A x=0$ is: $$ \text { Dimension }=5-\operatorname{rank}(A) $$ Given that this dimension is at least 2 : $$ 5-\operatorname{rank}(A) \geq 2 \Rightarrow \operatorname{rank}(A) \leq 3 $$ Now, we use the following property of matrix rank: $$ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{rank}\left(A^{2}\right) \leq \min (\operatorname{rank}(A), \operatorname{rank}(A))=\operatorname{rank}(A) \\ \Rightarrow \operatorname{rank}\left(A^{2}\right) \leq 3 \end{gathered} $$ Therefore, option (A) is correct. Since $\operatorname{rank}(A)<5$, the matrix $A$ is singular. Thus: $$ \operatorname{det}(A)=0 \Rightarrow \operatorname{det}\left(A^{2}\right)=(\operatorname{det} A)^{2}=0 $$ Therefore, option (D) is also correct. questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ real matrix that is singular (i.e., not invertible).
Let $x_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that the equation
$$
A x_{0}=b
$$
is satisfied.
Which of the following statements are true?

 

  1. There exists a vector $y_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $A^{T} y_{0}=b$.
  2. There exist infinitely many solutions to the equation $A x=b$.
  3. If $A^{T} x=0$, then $b^{T} x=0$.
  4. The solution to the equation $A x=b$ is unique.

options.label: A
options.text: There exists a vector $y_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $A^{T} y_{0}=b$.

options.label: B
options.text: There exist infinitely many solutions to the equation $A x=b$.

options.label: D
options.text: The solution to the equation $A x=b$ is unique.

questions.explanation: A. False : The equation $A x_{0}=b$ being solvable does not imply that the adjoint system $A^{T} y=b$ has a solution. B. True : Since $A$ is singular, its null space is nontrivial. So if a solution exists, there are infinitely many: $$ x=x_{0}+z \quad \text { for any } z \in \operatorname{Null}(A) $$ C.  True : Since $A x_{0}=b \Rightarrow b^{T}=x_{0}^{T} A^{T}$, if $A^{T} x=0$, then $b^{T} x=$ $x_{0}^{T} A^{T} x=0$. D.  False : A singular matrix cannot have a unique solution. If one solution exists, there are infinitely many. questions.explanation: Given that $A x=b$ has no solution, it means: $$ b \notin \operatorname{Col}(A) $$ i.e., $b$ is not in the column space of $A$. This implies that $A$ is not of full rank: $$ \operatorname{rank}(A)<n $$ Since $A$ is a square matrix of size $n \times n$, it is not invertible, and hence: $$ \operatorname{det}(A)=0 $$ So, (D) is true. The column space of $A$ is a proper subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, which means: $\exists$ infinitely many $c \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $c \notin \operatorname{Col}(A) \Rightarrow A x=c$ has no solution So, (B) is true. Now consider option (A). For $A x=c$ to have a unique solution, matrix $A$ must be invertible. But we already know $\operatorname{det}(A)=0 \Rightarrow A$ is not invertible. So such a $c$ does not exist. So, (A) is false. In option (C), let $y$ be the first column of $A$. Then $y \in \operatorname{Col}(A)$, so the system $A x=y$ has at least one solution. But since $A$ is not invertible, the solution is not unique. So, (C) is false. Fina

1 & 2 & 3 \\

$$
Consider the system of linear equations $A x=y$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. For which vectors $y$ does this system have a solution?
Which one of the following statements is true?

  1. The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}r & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]^{T}, r \in \mathbb{R}$
     
  2. The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}0 & s & 0\end{array}\right]^{T}, s \in \mathbb{R}$
     
  3. The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}0 & s & t\end{array}\right]^{T}, s, t \in \mathbb{R}$
     
  4. The system has a solution for all $y \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$

options.label: A
options.text: The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}r & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]^{T}, r \in \mathbb{R}$

options.label: B
options.text: The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}0 & s & 0\end{array}\right]^{T}, s \in \mathbb{R}$

options.label: C
options.text: The system has a solution only for $y=\left[\begin{array}{lll}0 & s & t\end{array}\right]^{T}, s, t \in \mathbb{R}$

questions.explanation: To determine whether $A x=y$ has a solution for all $y \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, we need to check whether the matrix $A$ is invertible. This is equivalent to checking whether $\operatorname{det}(A) \neq 0$. Compute the determinant: $$ \operatorname{det}(A)=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 5 & 1 \end{array}\right|=2\left|\begin{array}{ll} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 1 \end{array}\right|+5\left|\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 5 \end{array}\right| $$ $=2(2 \cdot 1-5 \cdot 3)+5(1 \cdot 5-(-1) \cdot 2)=2(2-15)+5(5+2)=2(-13)+5(7)=-26+35=9$ Since $\operatorname{det}(A)=9 \neq 0$, the matrix $A$ is invertible. Therefore, the system $A x=y$ has a solution for all $y \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$. GO Classes answered Jun 28, 2025 GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. Let $A$ be a $2 \times 2$ real matrix such that
$$
\operatorname{det}(A)=1 \quad \text { and } \quad \operatorname{tr}(A)=3 .

What is the value of $\operatorname{tr}\left(A^{2}\right)$ ?
questions.explanation: Explanation: Let $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ be the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$. We are given: $\operatorname{tr}(A)=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=3$ $\operatorname{det}(A)=\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}=1$ We are asked to compute $\operatorname{tr}\left(A^{2}\right)$. Note that the eigenvalues of $A^{2}$ are $\lambda_{1}^{2}$ and $\lambda_{2}^{2}$, so: $$ \operatorname{tr}\left(A^{2}\right)=\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2} $$ Now, use the identity: $$ \left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)^{2}=\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+2 \lambda_{1} \lambda_{2} $$ Substitute the known values: $$ 3^{2}=\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+2(1) \Rightarrow 9=\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}+2 \Rightarrow \lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}=9-2=7 $$ GO Classes answered Jun 28, 2025 • edited Jul 2, 2025 by GO Classes GO Classes comment Share Follow 0 reply Please log in or register to add a comment. \end{array}\right]
$$
Which of the following statements is true?

  1. $\operatorname{det}(M(t))$ is a polynomial of degree $3$ in $t$
     
  2. $\operatorname{det}(M(t))=0 \quad \forall t \in \mathbb{R}$
     
  3. $\operatorname{det}(M(t))=0$ for infinitely many values of $t \in \mathbb{R}$
     
  4. $\operatorname{det}(M(t))=0$ for exactly two values of $t \in \mathbb{R}$

options.label: A
options.text: $\operatorname{det}(M(t))$ is a polynomial of degree $3$ in $t$

questions.explanation: We compute the determinant of $M(t)$ : $$ \operatorname{det}(M(t))=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & t & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & t^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right| $$ Use cofactor expansion along the first row: $$ =1 \cdot\left|\begin{array}{cc} 1 & t^{2} \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right|-t \cdot\left|\begin{array}{cc} 1 & t^{2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right|+0 $$ Now compute: $$ =1\left(1 \cdot 1-1 \cdot t^{2}\right)-t\left(1 \cdot 1-0 \cdot t^{2}\right)=\left(1-t^{2}\right)-t=-t^{2}-t+1 $$ So, $$ \operatorname{det}(M(t))=-t^{2}-t+1 $$ This is a polynomial in $t$ of degree $2$ , not degree $3$ . : False. It's a degree $2$ polynomial, not degree $3$ . : False. The determinant is not always zero. : False . A degree $2$ polynomial can be zero at most at two real values. : True if the quadratic has two real roots. Let's check the discriminant: $$ (-1)^{2}-4(-1)(1)=1+4=5>0 $$ So the quadratic has two distinct real roots. GO Classes answered Jun 28, 2025 • edited

questions.explanation: To check diagonalizability, we compute the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda=2$ : $$ M-2 I=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right] \rightarrow \operatorname{RREF}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right] $$ This gives one free variable $\Rightarrow$ nullity $=1 \Rightarrow$ geometric multiplicity $=1$ Hence: Both eigenvalues have eigenspace of dimension $1$. $M$ is not diagonalizable (since geometric multiplicity $<$ algebraic multiplicity for $\lambda=2$ ).
